Welcome to the wonderful world on rubber monsters and spandex clad super heroes - otherwise known as Tokusatsu. Tokusatsu is a live action genre that makes heavy use of special effects and encompass many different series. This voat in particular focuses on the larger franchises, such as Super Sentai, Kamen Rider and Metal Heroes.

What series should I watch first?

It's entirely up to you, but many people will suggest looking for a series that catches your interest. The series are all different from one another, with wildly different tones and characters. If you don't like something in one series, it's easy to find a series you will like.

For Kamen Rider, the definite beginners series can be any of these three: W, Fourze and OOO. They give you a good idea of what to expect and all have good subs. (They're also connected to one another through a joint villainous faction, you don't really need to watch them in order despite this. If you care that much W came first, followed by Fourze and then OOO. This faction is addressed in a cross-over movie.)

For Super Sentai it's a crapshoot. Unlike Kamen Rider most Sentai series are similar in tone and pacing; there's also a lot more of them to choose from. An unfortunate consequence is that many series have sub-par subs that will effect your enjoyment of the show. (They can't all be winners after all.)

Many of the older series have great subs done by dedicated groups, while later series will have been done by Over-Time and Tv-nihon. I'll talk about which sub group you shoud use later, and where to find the series you want. If you're looking for something older, Megaranger is a fantastic first pick. If you're looking for something modern, Shinkenger is many people's first suggestion.

Fansubs: and why they're important

I've been slipping in mentions of subs throughout this guide, and you're probably wondering what I mean. A poor set of subtitles can completely ruin your enjoyment of the show. For example, when I first got into Sentai I started out by watching Go-Busters with TV-N subs, which turned out to be a horrible mistake. I dropped the show, but later came back to it with O-T subs and found it much more enjoyable.

As a newbie, you'll probably not be "in the know" about the sub groups that make up the fandom, and the associated reputations and qualities that come with using their translations. I'm going to run them down here.

Over-Time

A group focusing on mostly modern series, Over-Time is my top pick for new show releases. Fast, high quality encoding and well translated. Some argue that they localize idioms and such too much.

TV-Nihon

Usually what you see people using when they're making low quality youtube compilations. TV-Nihon is absolutely infamous for bad translations, poor quality video and horrific translator note abuse. They've gotten better in recent years, but the quality of their work varies so widely that I'd suggest not wasting your breath and going with someone else.

Just don't.

Grown Ups In Spandex

If you're looking for something retro, GUIS is your first port of call. They've subbed many different series, a lot of which are well worth a watch. No-nonsense subs that can be edited by the viewer.

MillionFoldCuriosity

Another group focusing on older shows, Ohranger, Megaranger and Gingaman are their most recent projects.

Scrubbers and Others

Sometimes there may not be a high quality sub available, and that's when you turn to your good friend, the scrubber. Scrubber's run through shows already subbed to improve them, these scrubs can also vary in quality. It's difficult to produce a list of Scrubbers, as many of them only produce one show, and also only appear on message boards like 4chan. Shop around a bit and you'll find something good.

Singular subbers are similar, certain individuals like MegaAnon have their own blog where you can see their releases, while others have fallen of the face of the earth leaving behind a mega link in their wake.

UEFI boot: how does that actually work, then?

Putting it quickly--UEFI reads the boot "signature" of an OS. A pirated OS in theory should not have this "signature."

Of course M$ products have a signature--Ubuntu has one also. I believe that other OSes are following. Still...it's a PITA to load Ubuntu on a UEFI machine--it helps to switch the BIOS to "legacy" before trying!

I've had no issues with that "signature" - but then again I don't install Windows (haven't since '07). MSFT also did get a lot of companies to put in additional data tables in firmware to store things like "this hardware was licensed for Windows".

From a little while back when I last tried out a few different distros there were actually quite a few that handled EFI quite well. I had graphical errors UEFI booting Ubuntu but that seemed to be a rare issue for people (I'm sure it's fixed by now though), Linux Mint worked with it perfectly, as did Sabyon and Bodhi (if I remember correctly). Others that didn't support a UEFI install (such as Debian) ran perfectly on a GPT partition and booted up trouble free regardless of my BIOS settings as long as I made the right selection from my boot menu of course.

There is also a UEFI bootloader called REFind that is quite nice for multiple OS installs with support for both UEFI and legacy / MBR installs.

That would only apply if your version of UEFI implemented secure boot, which isn't always the case. Most (if not all) self-build motherboards don't have a Secure Boot keystore, and don't have it enabled either. The article also points out the differences.

I never had difficulties install Ubuntu 12.04 on an UEFI system without Secure Boot.
'Fun' fact: switching an existing 32-bit BIOS install for a 64-bit UEFI install will require repartitioning (because you need a /boot partition).
